title: INFER: Learning Implicit Neural Frequency Response Fields for Confined Acoustic Environments
claim: A physically grounded frequency-domain forward model maps scene geometry to complex responses, trained end-to-end with perceptually weighted spectral supervision.
layout: Single wide row, left-to-right, with a feedback loop arrow along the bottom
description: A wide, left-to-right system diagram. On the left, a gray top-down car cabin sketch shows a speaker, a dashed reflected path and a direct path through two blue voxel boxes, V1 and V2, to a microphone. An arrow leads to a blue INR block of three vertical bars, labeled F_Θ(p, n, ...). Its output, S_i(f) with σ_i + jβ_i, enters a boxed 'Freq Domain Forward Modeling' panel. The panel has a TOF phase compensation spectrum multiplied by a complex exponential, and below it a KK-consistent complex attenuation strip with blue and orange segments over a decaying waveform. Output goes to a predicted spectrum H(f) and a ground-truth spectrum, both fed into a loss ‖H(f) − Ĥ(f)‖ * W(f). A frequency-weighting inset has green and pink bars. A feedback arrow returns to the INR. The eye lands first on the car and the blue INR block.
caption: System Overview. Illustration of our frequency-domain acoustic forward model. For each point sampled along rays cast from the microphone, the MLP predicts a frequency-domain signal and attenuation. A time-of-flight (TOF) based phase shift is applied to the signal and material-based absorption and phase shifts are applied to produce the final response by accumulating signal from all directions.
abstract: Neural acoustic fields often model time-domain impulse responses, which struggle to capture the frequency-selective wave behaviors that dominate confined, resonant environments. To address this, we propose INFER (Implicit Neural Frequency Response fields), a framework that directly learns continuous, complex-valued frequency response fields. Unlike prior time-domain methods, our frequency-first approach enables three key innovations: (1) end-to-end learning of frequency-specific attenuation and phase delay in 3D space; (2) a physics-based Kramers–Kronig consistency constraint that causally regularizes attenuation and phase delay; and (3) perceptual and hardware-aware spectral supervision that prioritizes critical auditory bands. We evaluate INFER across diverse settings, ranging from standard room-scale benchmarks (MeshRIR, RAF) to challenging, highly reverberant environments like real car cabins. Our approach significantly outperforms time- and hybrid-domain baselines, reducing average magnitude and phase reconstruction errors by over 39\% and 51\%, respectively, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy in modeling complex acoustic spaces.
